abstract: Siddiq and Zhang study whether generative AI has changed how online labor markets value workers' human capital. Using 49,610 Upwork worker profiles and 2.26 million contracts spanning 2021Q1–2026Q1, they represent worker profiles with 384-dimensional text embeddings (MiniLM) and use Shapley regression values to measure the predictive importance of three human capital blocks (self-presentation, credentials, reputation) and price in explaining quarterly contract volume. Embedding the analysis in a difference-in-differences design around the November 2022 release of ChatGPT — with occupational AI exposure (Eloundou et al. 2024 'E1' scores) as continuous treatment — they find that the combined importance of human capital signals fell ~7.8% in the most AI-exposed categories, while price importance rose ~1.1%. Effects grow over time: by 2025Q2–2026Q1 the human capital decline reaches 10.1% and the price rise reaches 1.8%. Two additional tests support a 'labor commoditization' mechanism (rather than mere quality-signaling): the demand premium attached to workers with strong pre-AI human capital signals compresses by 6.2% (10.3% late period), and demand reallocates from higher- to lower-priced workers by 3.2% (7.9% late period). The authors argue this is the first empirical demonstration of Fukui–Nakamura–Steinsson (2026) labor commoditization in a real labor market.
keyFindings: Contract volume for max-AI-exposure workers (e.g., Translation) fell ~7.0% post-ChatGPT vs. unexposed workers (e.g., Audio Production); 9.6% in late 2025Q2–2026Q1 window
Combined importance of self-presentation, credentials, and reputation in predicting hire-volume fell ~7.8% (10.1% late) in max-exposure categories
Importance of posted hourly price for predicting hires rose ~1.1% (1.8% late) — opposite sign to human capital decline
Demand premium attached to workers with strong pre-AI human capital signals compressed by 6.2% (10.3% late) in max-exposure categories
Demand reallocated from higher- to lower-priced workers by 3.2% (7.9% late), distinguishing commoditization from a quality-signaling story

Decline in importance is spread roughly evenly across all three human capital blocks — not concentrated in worker-authored 'cheap talk' fields (self-presentation), but also affects externally validated credentials (degrees, employment history) and platform reputation (badges, prior client feedback)
Effects are not confined to the immediate ChatGPT release — they continue to widen more than three years after the shock, suggesting the market has not yet re-equilibrated
methodology: Balanced panel of 49,610 active Upwork workers across 21 quarters (Jan 2021 – Mar 2026), drawn from a March 2026 snapshot. Demand outcome is log(1 + quarterly contracts). Each worker profile is split into self-presentation, credentials, reputation, and price blocks (1,177 total features after combining 384-dim text embeddings with structured variables). Quarter-specific OLS prediction model produces out-of-fold (5-fold CV) predicted demand. Block-level Shapley values (16 sub-models per quarter) decompose predicted demand exactly into block-specific contributions. AI exposure assigned at the worker level from Eloundou et al. (2024) E1 scores via LLM-based mapping of Upwork's 102 subcategories to O*NET occupations; rescaled by max (0.8 for Translation) so effects are interpretable as 'fully exposed vs. fully unexposed.' Inference via worker-level bootstrap (100 reps) plus subcategory-level placebo permutations (2,000 reps). Robustness: results replicate under ridge regression, XGBoost, Arctic 2.0-M embeddings, and price-control specifications.
qualifiers: Worker profile fields (titles, descriptions, credentials, posted hourly rate) are observed only in a single March 2026 snapshot, so post-shock profile changes cannot be ruled out; authors argue this biases estimates toward zero. Workers who deleted their accounts before March 2026 are not observed, so results apply to workers whose profiles remained on the platform. Reputation is the only time-varying block. Cover letters, search-result ordering, and worker proposals are not observed. The 'E1' exposure score is task-based and category-level, not occupation-level worker behavior. Pre-trend tests fail to reject parallel trends for the three human capital blocks but reject for price (p=0.01) — the authors note the deviation is small relative to the post-effect (~1/7). Findings are empirically distinct from quality-signaling because demand shifts *toward* lower-priced workers, not the opposite. Generalization to non-online labor markets is suggested but not tested.
